# Data collection

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/

> Two ways to record touch together with vision and actions, by teleoperation or with a handheld UMI gripper.

A tactile demonstration records what the sensor feels, what the camera sees and what the gripper does, all at the same moments. There are two ways to collect one.

**[Simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/)**

A third source: generate visuo-tactile demonstrations in Isaac Sim, without physical hardware.

**New to robot learning?** Start with teleoperation. It is the lowest-cost setup and uses the sensor exactly as these docs set it up.

## What each source records

| Source | What you get | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Teleoperation (LeFlexiTac) | A LeRobot dataset: the tactile map, camera and joint states of each frame, at 30 fps | [LeFlexiTac docs](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/docs.html#reproduction) |
| Handheld UMI (Touch in the Wild) | GoPro video and tactile JSON logs recorded with ROS 2, aligned by a SLAM pipeline into one `dataset.zarr.zip` | [README: SLAM pipeline](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#creating-a-dataset-with-the-slam-pipeline) |
| Simulation (Isaac Sim) | One `.npz` per demonstration: the four pads' tactile maps, camera images, joint states and actions | [Its keys and shapes](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#web) |

## Teleoperation

You move a leader arm and the follower robot copies it, so the recorded actions are the robot's own. The open setup is [LeFlexiTac](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/), which adds FlexiTac to [LeRobot](https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot) on the low-cost SO-100/101 arm.

- **Robot:** SO-100/101 leader and follower arms, a camera and a Linux machine
- **Sensor:** One standard FlexiTac sensor (32 × 12), on the follower's 3D-printed moving jaw only
- **Reader:** PyFlexiTac, with the firmware from [Stream the sensor](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/)
- **Output:** A LeRobot dataset: the tactile map next to the camera and joint states, at 30 fps

*Sample: Recording a LeFlexiTac demonstration. The leader arm (right) drives the follower, and the screen shows the tactile map and camera view going into the dataset.*

The full guide is **steps 01–08** of the [LeFlexiTac docs](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/docs.html#reproduction), from building the robot to collecting data. In short:

1. **Build the arm and the tactile jaw**
   Assemble the arms from the [SO-ARM100 guide](https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100), then print LeFlexiTac's Moving Jaw and Wrist Roll and fit them.
2. **Install LeFlexiTac**
   Install the [fork](https://github.com/TNA001-AI/lerobot_tactile) from source in a Python 3.12 environment. `pip install lerobot` gives you upstream LeRobot, which has no tactile support.
3. **Calibrate the arms and mount the sensor**
   Calibrate and test teleoperation with [LeRobot's SO-101 walkthrough](https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/il_robots), then mount the sensor and confirm it with `flexitac-heatmap`.
4. **Record demonstrations**
   Record with `lerobot-record` and the `so_tactile_follower` robot type.

Then train [ACT or Diffusion Policy](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/#leflexitac), or [Pi0.5 and SmolVLA](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/vla/#leflexitac), on your dataset.

## UMI data

You hold a [UMI](https://github.com/real-stanford/universal_manipulation_interface)-style gripper and do the task yourself, indoors or outdoors, with no robot. A GoPro on the gripper records vision, and a FlexiTac sensor on each soft finger records touch. The open setup is [Touch in the Wild](https://binghao-huang.github.io/touch_in_the_wild/) (NeurIPS 2025). Its authors used it to collect more than 2,700 demonstrations across 43 tasks in 12 environments.

> **Before you build: it needs different firmware**
>
> Touch in the Wild reads the boards with its own code, not PyFlexiTac: a ROS 2 node while recording, and serial readers when running a policy. Both expect the older **text** output, 16 lines of 32 numbers per frame. The firmware in [Stream the sensor](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/stream/#flash) sends **binary** frames instead, so a board flashed from these docs won't work with Touch in the Wild as it is, and its repositories don't include matching firmware. Ask in its [issues](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild/issues) or on the [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms) before you build.

- **Gripper:** The UMI handheld gripper with Touch in the Wild's modifications, and a GoPro Hero 9
- **Sensors:** Two standard FlexiTac sensors (32 × 12), one on each soft finger
- **Reader:** ROS 2 Humble on Ubuntu 22.04, with older text-format firmware (see the caution above)
- **Output:** GoPro video and tactile streams, turned into a training dataset by a SLAM pipeline
- **Shared data:** The [Touch in the Wild dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/binghaohuang-robot/touch_in_the_wild-dataset). The pretraining set alone is about 88 GB.

Outdoors

Shelf

Workbench

*Sample data: Three demonstrations from Touch in the Wild: the GoPro's fish-eye view, with the left and right fingers' tactile maps below it.*

1. **Build the gripper**
   Build the UMI gripper, then apply Touch in the Wild's top plate and finger holders and add the two sensors. [Gripper guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Gxd2PzVo-sH_XbvnVw_r3eI5i3I3t0rr7JdhpN1PJMA/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.dcjpnwh7wh40)
2. **Set up the recording laptop**
   Give each reading board a fixed device name, then install the ROS 2 tactile packages. [Device names](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild-data-collection#udev) · [ROS 2 setup](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild-data-collection#ros)
3. **Collect demonstrations**
   Record the tactile streams with ROS 2 while the GoPro films. [Data collection protocol](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild-data-collection#protocol)
4. **Turn the recordings into a dataset**
   Run the SLAM pipeline on the session folder. [README: SLAM pipeline](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#creating-a-dataset-with-the-slam-pipeline)

Next, [pretrain the visuo-tactile encoder](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/pretraining/#touch-in-the-wild) or start from the released one, then train a [Diffusion Policy](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/#touch-in-the-wild).

## Good data, either way

- **Check every session before you record.** Run `flexitac-stream` or the heatmap and press each sensor: every row and column should respond. A dead row can't be fixed in data you've already recorded.
- **Mount on something slightly soft,** such as a fin-ray finger, so contact spreads over several taxels.
- **Keep the cable still at the connector.** Route the flat cable so it doesn't flex while the gripper moves.
- **Redo the baseline calibration after mounting.** The mount itself changes the resting baseline.
- **In your own code, record `raw` and the baseline,** not only `normalized`: it is scaled per frame and hides how hard the contact is ([why](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#normalized)).
- **Keep touch in sync.** LeFlexiTac records touch into the same dataset frames as the camera and joints, so train and run a policy at the frame rate you recorded at. Touch in the Wild shows a QR code to the camera before each demonstration to line up video and touch. In your own setup, record with PyFlexiTac's `sensor.read()`, which returns every received frame in order, and keep each frame's `timestamp_s` ([Read frames in Python](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#python)). It's host time, so USB delay is part of it.
- **Choose the tactile rate once.** The sensor streams around 100 fps, and a dataset usually samples it at the camera's rate: LeFlexiTac records at 30 fps. Either take the newest frame at each step (`read_latest()`) or keep every frame (`read()`) and resample later, but don't mix the two.
- **Look at a few episodes before you record many.** Play the tactile maps back next to the video: contact should appear when the gripper closes, and no taxel should stay stuck.
- **Another gripper?** [FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/) designs a sensor that fits it.


---

# Tactile representation

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/

> Give touch to a policy as a 2D map per pad, or as 3D tactile points in one point cloud with the camera's, shown on a simulated two-armed demonstration.

Every FlexiTac frame is a grid of numbers, one per taxel: 12 rows by 32 columns on a standard sensor ([why 12 × 32 and not 32 × 12](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/#array-shape)). Before a policy can learn from it, you choose how to represent it. There are two ways, and the difference is whether touch knows *where* it happens.

  [2D tactile maps](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/#2d) *Local contact patterns*

A fixed sensor layout, CNN encoders, and the easiest way into imitation learning.

- **Policy gets:** One 12 × 32 map per pad
- **Encoder:** MLP or small CNN
- **Used by:** [LeFlexiTac](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/), [Touch in the Wild](https://binghao-huang.github.io/touch_in_the_wild/)

  [3D tactile points](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/#3d) *Spatially grounded contact*

Geometric reasoning, visuo-tactile fusion, and manipulation across poses.

- **Policy gets:** One 3D point per taxel
- **Encoder:** PointNet or similar
- **Used by:** [3D-ViTac](https://binghao-huang.github.io/3D-ViTac/), [VT-Refine](https://binghao-huang.github.io/vt_refine/)

A conceptual guide. Which works better for your task still has to be tested on it.

## 2D: a map per pad

The firmware sends each frame as `uint8[12][32]`, row by row ([PyFlexiTac](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#python)). Subtract each taxel's resting baseline and scale, and every reading lies between 0 and 1. Keep the numbers on their grid, colour them by value, and the array is an image:

![A 12 by 32 grid of readings, mostly 0; the pressed taxels form a slanted band at one end of the pad](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/tactile-map.svg)

*Simulated: One pad at one moment: 384 readings on its 12 × 32 grid (row, column). The pressed taxels form a band where the plug lies across the pad. From the simulated demonstration below (right arm, left finger), at the same moment as its 3D view; the simulator reports force divided by 10 N.*

A policy can take the map in two ways:

- **As a vector.** Flatten the 384 readings into one list and feed it to an MLP. It's the simplest input, but the network has to learn which taxels are neighbours.
- **As an image.** Keep the grid and use a small CNN, as for a one-channel camera image, so a contact's shape looks the same wherever it falls on the pad. LeFlexiTac does this: three 3 × 3 convolution layers with pooling turn each map into 256 features, which become extra tokens for ACT, or part of Diffusion Policy's conditioning ([encoder](https://github.com/TNA001-AI/lerobot_tactile/blob/6e59779ac4a711155474477e7ab6997d7160ead0/src/lerobot/policies/tactile/encoder.py)). Touch in the Wild treats touch as images too: its pre-training learns to rebuild masked tactile images from the camera image.

Settle two things before you record:

- **How you normalize.** PyFlexiTac's `normalized` divides each frame by its own peak once there is contact, so it keeps the shape of a contact but not how hard it is ([details](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/pyflexitac/#normalized)). LeFlexiTac records these maps, and VT-Refine uses the same kind of rule: each pad is scaled by its own peak once it is pressed. If force matters, record `raw` and the baseline too. Either way, normalize the same way in training and on the robot.
- **Which pad is which.** Keep the pads in a fixed order and orientation. Touch in the Wild stores its two pads side by side, as one 12 × 64 map per frame.

**A map doesn't say where the pad is.** The same line of contact means something different when the gripper is turned or the object is higher. Given the joint angles and the pad's fixed mounting, a policy can still infer where the contact is, but it has to learn that from data. 3D tactile points put it in the data.

## 3D: tactile points

[3D-ViTac](https://binghao-huang.github.io/3D-ViTac/) (CoRL 2024) puts every taxel in the same 3D frame as the camera's points, so fingers, contacts and objects share one point cloud. [VT-Refine](https://binghao-huang.github.io/vt_refine/) (CoRL 2025) does the same on the two-armed ALOHA robot. The viewer shows one plug–socket demonstration from [FlexiTac's Isaac Sim simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#isaac-sim), with a pad on each of ALOHA's four fingers.

![One frame of a simulated plug–socket insertion: the camera picture in a corner, grey camera points of the grippers, plug and socket, and four pads of tactile points with the pressed taxels in orange](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/assets/img/isaac-frame.webp)

Simulated: The right arm holds the plug over the socket in the left hand. **Inset:** the camera's picture. **Grey:** the points the same camera sees, 1,024 of them here so they read clearly (VT-Refine keeps 512). **Purple to yellow:** the four pads' 1,536 tactile points, colored by reading on the viridis scale (purple where nothing presses). On the right, the same readings as 2D maps; below, the joint positions the policy also gets. Drag to turn it, **Camera view** goes back to the camera, and play runs the demonstration at its recorded 30 frames a second.

### How a frame is built

1. **Proprioception**
   Read the 16 joint positions of both arms and grippers: per arm, 6 joints and 2 fingers. They do two jobs. Forward kinematics turns them into each pad's pose, which the next step needs, and they go to the policy as an input of their own, through a small MLP. (That is the design in both papers. VT-Refine's released ALOHA config leaves this input out and uses the cloud alone.)
2. **Tactile points**
   Each taxel has a fixed spot on its pad: a 12 × 32 grid, 2 mm apart. Moving the grid by its pad's pose puts every taxel in the table's frame (its origin is the centre of the table). Each tactile point carries its reading. Untouched taxels stay, with a reading of 0, so there are always 4 × 384 = 1,536 of them, and they also show where the fingers are.
3. **Camera points**
   The depth camera's image becomes 3D points in the same table frame. Points outside a box around the workspace are dropped, and 512 of the rest are kept. They carry no colour.
4. **One point cloud**
   Both sets go into one cloud of 2,048 points. Each point has five numbers: x, y, z, the reading (0 for camera points), and a flag that tells the two kinds apart (0 for the camera, 1 for touch).
5. **Encoder and policy**
   A PointNet runs the same small network on every point, then keeps the maximum of each feature over all points, so the order of the points doesn't matter. With the joint features, the result conditions a Diffusion Policy. In VT-Refine it sees the last two frames, predicts the next 16 steps of target joint positions, runs 8 of them, then looks again. 3D-ViTac uses PointNet++.

### In simulation

VT-Refine builds the same observation in simulation, so a policy trained on real demonstrations can keep training there with reinforcement learning. The taxel grid is laid on each simulated pad, the physics engine gives the pad's pose, and each reading comes from how far the taxel presses into the object, normalized with the same rule as the real pads. Noise is added to the simulated camera points only. See [Tactile simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#vt-refine).

The viewer above comes from FlexiTac's Isaac Sim simulation in the same way. Its tactile sensors give each taxel's position and reading directly. The picture and the camera points come from the simulated camera's color and depth images, so the cloud has no sensor noise, and the table is cropped away just above its surface, as on a real robot ([recording script](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/blob/main/doc/_src/tools/isaac_sample.py)).

## The data

VT-Refine's pre-training data, its real-robot demonstrations, stores every step as plain arrays. For the ALOHA tasks:

| Array | Shape per step | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `point_cloud` | 3 × 512 | Camera points: x, y, z in metres, in the table's frame |
| `tactile_points` | 4 × 1,536 | The four pads' 384 taxels each: x, y, z and the reading (0 to 1, each pad scaled by its own peak) |
| `joint_states` | 16 | Joint positions: per arm, 6 joints and 2 fingers, left arm first, scaled to −1…1 |
| `actions` | 16 | Target joint positions, in the same order and scale |
| `traj_lengths` | one per demonstration | Its number of steps, to split the arrays into demonstrations |

The pads are in the order left arm left finger, left arm right finger, right arm left finger, right arm right finger. `normalization.pth`, next to each `train.npz`, holds the ranges to turn joint values and actions back into radians and metres.

To get the 2D maps back from this data, or to build the five-channel cloud yourself:

```python
import numpy as np

d = np.load("train.npz")                    # plain arrays; no pickle needed
t = 0                                        # a step: any index below len(d["actions"])
pc, tac = d["point_cloud"][t], d["tactile_points"][t]   # (3, 512), (4, 1536)

# 2D: each pad's 384 points are stored column by column
maps = tac[3].reshape(4, 32, 12).transpose(0, 2, 1)       # (4, 12, 32)

# 3D: x, y, z, reading, flag
cloud = np.concatenate([
    np.vstack([pc,  np.zeros((2, 512))]),    # camera points: reading 0, flag 0
    np.vstack([tac, np.ones((1, 1536))]),    # tactile points: reading, flag 1
], axis=1)                                   # (5, 2048)
```

The data is about 909 MB, under CC BY-NC 4.0. Download it with `data/fetch_vt-refine_data.sh` from the [VT-Refine repository](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine).

# Imitation learning with touch (in progress)

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/imitation-learning/

> ACT and Diffusion Policy.

> **Coming soon**
>
> We're writing a full guide to this topic. Until then, both [data-collection setups](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/) come with training code you can use today.

## Available today

### LeFlexiTac: ACT and Diffusion Policy

LeFlexiTac trains policies on the LeRobot datasets you [record with it](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/#teleoperation). Touch is an extra input, switched on with `--policy.use_tactile=true`. On tube insertion, peg-in-hole and pen retrieval from a bag, the tactile policies beat their vision-only versions in every reported comparison ([results](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/)).

Train with and without touch (`--policy.use_tactile=true` / `false`) on a Linux machine with a CUDA GPU, then roll the checkpoint out on the arm. Train and run a policy at the same frame rate you recorded at. Steps 09–10 of the [LeFlexiTac docs](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/docs.html#reproduction) have the training and evaluation commands, and the same page ends with practical tips on calibration, camera placement and frame rates.

### Touch in the Wild: Diffusion Policy

Touch in the Wild trains a Diffusion Policy conditioned on its [pretrained visuo-tactile encoder](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/pretraining/#touch-in-the-wild), then runs it on a uFactory xArm 850 with the same fingers and sensors.

**To run policies you need:** a uFactory xArm 850 with the xArm Gripper, the printed finger holder and GoPro mount from the [gripper guide](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Gxd2PzVo-sH_XbvnVw_r3eI5i3I3t0rr7JdhpN1PJMA/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.dcjpnwh7wh40), an HDMI capture card for the GoPro feed, and an NVIDIA GPU for training. [README: Training](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#training-diffusionpolicies) · [Real-world deployment](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild#realworld-deployment)

The pretraining set alone is about 88 GB. # Tactile simulation

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/

> Simulate FlexiTac pads in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, then replay tactile trajectories and record visuo-tactile demonstrations in the browser. Plus VT-Refine, the sim fine-tuning research behind it.

The simulation lets you work with touch without any hardware. Simulated pads give the same 12 × 32 taxel grid as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor, on the fingers of a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The current release is the **FlexiTac tactile simulation in Isaac Sim**, which this page shows you how to build and run. It uses the same bimanual plug–socket setup and the same pad layout as **VT-Refine**, the research on fine-tuning visuo-tactile policies in simulation, whose own code runs on the older Isaac Gym.

|  | Isaac Sim simulation (current release) | VT-Refine (research code) |
|---|---|---|
| **Simulator** | Isaac Sim 6.2 with Isaac Lab 3.0 | Isaac Gym Preview (TacSL build), in Docker |
| **Robot and task** | Bimanual ALOHA robot, plug–socket insertion | ALOHA-style tabletop arms and a two-arm Kinova robot, plug–socket insertion |
| **Simulated pads** | 12 × 32 taxels at 2 mm on all four fingers | 12 × 32 at 2 mm on the ALOHA setup |
| **What you do with it** | Replay trajectories with live tactile heatmaps; teleoperate in the browser and record demonstrations | Pre-train a visuo-tactile policy, then fine-tune it with reinforcement learning |
| **Code** | [FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation) | [NVlabs/vt-refine](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine) |

## Build the Isaac Sim simulation

The repository is an Isaac Lab tree with two additions: a tactile sensor for FlexiTac pads, and an ALOHA environment whose four fingers each carry a simulated pad.

**You need:** a Linux x86_64 computer (Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with an NVIDIA RTX GPU and a driver of version 580.65 or newer, plus git and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Isaac Sim, PyTorch and Isaac Lab take about 30 GB. The trajectory viewer opens a desktop window; the browser interface can run headless. No FlexiTac hardware is needed.

1. **Clone the repository**
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation.git
   cd FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation
   ```
2. **Create a Python 3.12 environment**
   *FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*
   ```bash
   uv venv --python 3.12 --seed env_isaaclab
   source env_isaaclab/bin/activate
   ```
3. **Install Isaac Sim 6.2 and PyTorch**
   The CUDA 13 build of PyTorch is the one Isaac Lab 3.0 pins:
   *FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*
   ```bash
   uv pip install "isaacsim[all,extscache]==6.2.0" --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com --index-strategy unsafe-best-match
   uv pip install -U torch==2.11.0 torchvision==0.26.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
   ```
   The first launch asks you to accept the NVIDIA Omniverse EULA; `export OMNI_KIT_ACCEPT_EULA=YES` accepts it ahead of time.
4. **Install Isaac Lab and the viewer dependencies**
   `core` installs Isaac Lab's packages, including the FlexiTac sensor, and `visualizer[kit]` the Isaac Sim window:
   *FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*
   ```bash
   sudo apt install cmake build-essential
   ./isaaclab.sh -i core
   ./isaaclab.sh -i 'visualizer[kit]'
   uv pip install viser opencv-python
   ```

These steps follow the repository's [installation guide](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation#%EF%B8%8F-installation) as of November 2026. If the two differ, the README is the source of truth. For Isaac Sim 5.1 and Isaac Lab 2.3, use the repository's [`isaacsim-5.1` branch](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/tree/isaacsim-5.1) and its README.

## Replay a trajectory with touch

Replay an episode from the bundled sample dataset. The ALOHA robot repeats the recorded motion, and a separate window shows the four finger pads as live tactile heatmaps.

*FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*

```bash
./isaaclab.sh -p Isaacsim_tactile_env/reply_with_tactile.py \
    --dataset_npz Isaacsim_tactile_env/data/dataset_train.npz \
    --normalization_pth Isaacsim_tactile_env/data/dataset_normalizer.npz \
    --episode_idx 3 \
    --replay_key joint_states \
    --steps_per_frame 3
```

The script really is named `reply_with_tactile.py`. Change `--episode_idx` to replay another episode, and add `--headless` to run without the Isaac Sim window.

## Teleoperate and record in the browser

Start the web interface, then open **http://localhost:8080**:

*FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/*

```bash
./isaaclab.sh -p Isaacsim_tactile_env/viser_interface.py \
    --headless \
    --enable_cameras
```

Drag the handle on each end effector to move the two arms, and open or close each gripper with its buttons. The page shows the four tactile heatmaps, the simulated camera and the robot state as you work. **Reset** puts the plug and socket back at the start with a slightly randomized wrist orientation.

**Start Recording** and **Stop Recording** save each demonstration as one `.npz` file in `Isaacsim_tactile_env/output/trajectories/`. Each file holds:

| Key | Shape | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `tactile` | (T, 4, 12, 32) | The four pads, in the order left arm left finger, left arm right finger, right arm left finger, right arm right finger |
| `joint_pos`, `joint_vel` | (T, 16) | Joint positions and velocities of both arms |
| `actions` | (T, 16) | Per arm: target position (3), quaternion (4), gripper (1) |
| `plug_pose`, `socket_pose` | (T, 7) | Object position and wxyz quaternion |
| `rgb` | (T, 480, 640, 3) | Camera images |

## How the simulated pad works

Each finger has a pad with a 12 × 32 grid of taxels at 2 mm pitch, the same layout as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor. On every step, [NVIDIA Warp](https://github.com/NVIDIA/warp) measures how far each taxel has pushed into the object's mesh. That depth becomes a spring force, `clamp(stiffness × depth, 0, max_force)`, which is then divided by `max_force` so each reading lies between 0 and 1. The taxels sit 1.4 mm in front of the pad's face, so a reading starts just before the object touches it; lower `normal_offset` (or pass `--normal_offset` to either script) for smaller contact patches. The grid size, spacing, `normal_offset` (0.0029 m from the pad's mid-plane), `stiffness` (5000) and `max_force` (10) are settings in [`AlohaTactileEnvCfg`](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/blob/3d8006656dcd916f0af4c653f0aa5fba6f3ace6e/Isaacsim_tactile_env/aloha_tactile_cfg.py#L53-L64).

> **What it does not model yet**
>
> - The pads on the left arm sense only the socket, and the pads on the right arm only the plug. Touching anything else, such as the table, gives no signal.
> - Readings are normalized from 0 to 1, not calibrated to a real sensor's output.
> - The environment is built around the ALOHA robot. Using another gripper or pad layout means changing the code; there is no guide for that yet.

## VT-Refine

[VT-Refine](https://binghao-huang.github.io/vt_refine/) (CoRL 2025) trains bimanual assembly policies in three stages, from real to sim and back to real. It first trains a diffusion policy on about 30 real demonstrations per task. Each demonstration records FlexiTac pads on all four fingers together with a camera point cloud, the representation from [3D-ViTac](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/#3d). Next it fine-tunes that policy in a simulated copy of the setup with large-scale, GPU-parallel reinforcement learning. Finally it moves the policy back to the real robot. The tasks are plug–socket insertions done in mid-air.

The repository has the simulation and training side: a Docker environment, the simulated environments with their tactile model, training configs, and a script that downloads about 909 MB of pre-training data. It does not include trained checkpoints or code for collecting data or running on a real robot.

1. **Install with Docker**
   Clone with submodules and build the image, which installs the TacSL build of Isaac Gym. [README: Installation](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#installation)
2. **Pre-train the visuo-tactile policy**
   Download the data and train the diffusion policy. [README: Pre-training](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#pre-training)
3. **Fine-tune in simulation**
   Evaluate the pre-trained policy in simulation, then fine-tune it with reinforcement learning. [README: Evaluation](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#evaluation---pre-training) · [Fine-tuning](https://github.com/NVlabs/vt-refine#fine-tuning)

> **License and simulator**
>
> The VT-Refine repository is under the NVIDIA License (non-commercial research and evaluation only), and its pre-training data under CC BY-NC 4.0. The submodules it pulls in, with the simulated environments, the tactile model and the training code, are MIT-licensed. It runs on Isaac Gym, which NVIDIA no longer develops. For new work, start from the [Isaac Sim simulation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/simulation/#isaac-sim) above.

## On these pages

- The 3D sensor on the [Introduction](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/) is rendered from the V2 Gerbers on the UMI soft finger from [HandUMI](https://github.com/murobotics-ai/handumi-hw) (Apache-2.0), and shown with [model-viewer](https://modelviewer.dev/) (Apache-2.0).
- The FPC drawings, the exploded view and the colours of the boards follow [Learn FlexiTac](https://flexitac.github.io/learn/).
- The "What you'll build" renders on [Quickstart](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/) are made the same way: the sensor from the V2 Gerbers on the HandUMI finger, the reading board from its Gerbers and parts list, the Arduino Nano laid out as in Learn FlexiTac, and the FFC extenders modeled on Adafruit's product photos.
- The sample clips on [Data collection](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/data-collection/) come from the [LeFlexiTac](https://tna001-ai.github.io/LeFlexiTac/) and [Touch in the Wild](https://binghao-huang.github.io/touch_in_the_wild/) project pages.
- The point cloud viewer and the tactile map on [Tactile representation](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/robot-learning/tactile-representation/) show one plug–socket demonstration replayed in [FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation) (Isaac Sim 6.2 and Isaac Lab 3.0): the ALOHA robot with UMI-style fingers, the WarpSdf tactile sensors, and an RTX camera for the pictures and the depth behind the camera points.
- The xArm render in the Introduction's Design card comes from the [FlexiTac-Gen](https://flexitac.github.io/flexitac-gen/) library: the gripper is UFACTORY's 3D model, and the sensor is the FlexiTac V2 design.
- The FlexiTac hardware is © 2026 Columbia University, licensed under [CC BY-NC 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/). PyFlexiTac is MIT-licensed. Other projects carry their own licenses.

# Contributing

URL: https://flexitac.github.io/doc/contributing/

> Share your robot, list your paper, improve these docs or the code, and report bugs. Where each contribution goes and what it needs.

FlexiTac grows through the people who build with it. Whatever you made, a mount, a fix or a whole robot, it helps the next person. Each kind of contribution goes to the project that owns it:

| You want to | Go to |
|---|---|
| Ask a question or show work in progress | [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms) |
| Show a robot you built with FlexiTac | [Share your robot](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/contributing/#robot) |
| List your paper or project | [Add your paper](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/contributing/#papers) |
| Fix a page or add what you tested | [Improve these docs](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/contributing/#docs) |
| Report a bug or improve the code | [Report a bug](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/contributing/#code) |

## Share your robot

Built FlexiTac into your own gripper, hand or robot? Send it in with the [Share your robot](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/issues/new?template=share-your-robot.yml) form.

1. **Submit**
   The form asks for a name, two to four sentences on what you built, which sensor (the standard V2, one from FlexiTac-Gen or your own design), how far along it is, a photo or short video, and how to credit you. A landscape photo works best: it becomes your tile. Links to your project page, paper, code or CAD are optional.
2. **We review**
   A maintainer checks every submission and may ask a question or two in the issue thread. Nothing appears on the site before it's approved.
3. **Featured**
   Approved robots appear in the Community row under [A growing tactile ecosystem](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/#ecosystem) on the docs home, with credit to you and a link to your project.

The submission is a public GitHub issue. To share unpublished work privately first, ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms).

## Add your paper or project

[Awesome FlexiTac](https://binghao-huang.github.io/Awesome-FlexiTac/) lists the papers and projects built with flexible tactile arrays. Add yours by [opening an issue or pull request](https://github.com/binghao-huang/Awesome-FlexiTac/issues), as its [contributing guide](https://github.com/binghao-huang/Awesome-FlexiTac/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) describes.

## Improve these docs

Tested a new sensor/board combination, found a step that tripped you up, or solved a problem on Discord that [Troubleshooting](https://flexitac.github.io/doc/get-started/troubleshooting/) doesn't cover? Every page has an **Edit page** link at the bottom. It opens the page's Markdown on GitHub, where you can propose your change as a pull request.

For bigger changes, such as a new page or images, work in a clone of [FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io):

1. **Edit the Markdown**
   The pages are in `doc/_src/pages/`. A new page also needs its slug in `NAV` at the top of `doc/_src/build.py`, which sets the sidebar order.
2. **Rebuild and check**
   ```bash
   # Python 3.9+, standard library only
   python3 doc/_src/build.py
   # Fails on stale HTML or a broken link, anchor or image
   python3 doc/_src/build.py --check
   ```
3. **Preview**
   From the repository root, run `python3 -m http.server 8000` and open `http://localhost:8000/doc/`.
4. **Open a pull request**
   Commit both the Markdown and the generated HTML.

The [docs source README](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/blob/main/doc/_src/README.md) lists the Markdown you can use, and how to store images and videos. Three rules matter most:

- **One source of truth.** These docs cover the getting-started path and link out. Detailed procedures stay in the repository that owns them: summarize them here and link the original.
- **Only verified facts.** Version numbers, pin counts, frame sizes and prices come from a linked source or from something you tested. Say how you tested it.
- **Credit and licenses.** Keep the authors' credit and each project's license. Images need permission from whoever owns them.

## Report a bug or improve the code

Not sure where a problem comes from? Ask on [Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms) first. Otherwise open an issue, or send a pull request, in the repository that owns the code:

| Problem with | Repository |
|---|---|
| Sensor design, reading board, `32_16_fast.ino`, FlexiTac-Gen | [FlexiTac/FlexiTac](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac/issues) |
| `flexitac-*` commands, the Python API, `flexitac-flash` firmware | [WT-MM/PyFlexiTac](https://github.com/WT-MM/PyFlexiTac/issues) |
| LeFlexiTac: teleoperation and training on the SO-100/101 | [TNA001-AI/lerobot_tactile](https://github.com/TNA001-AI/lerobot_tactile/issues) |
| Touch in the Wild | [XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild](https://github.com/XinyueZhuXY/touch_in_the_wild/issues) |
| The Isaac Sim tactile simulation | [binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation](https://github.com/binghao-huang/FlexiTac-IsaacSim-Simulation/issues) |
| These docs | [FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac.github.io/issues) |

A report anyone can act on includes: sensor version or geometry, reading board (32 × 16 or 32 × 32), which firmware you flashed and its settings, OS and Python version, the exact command you ran, the full output, and a photo of the connections.

## Stay in touch

- **[Discord](https://discord.gg/6gw887Vxms):** questions, help, and builds in progress.
- **WeChat:** the group's [QR code](https://flexitac.github.io/static/images/qr.jpg).
- **Star** [FlexiTac on GitHub](https://github.com/FlexiTac/FlexiTac) so others can find it.
